extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / scientists conducting animal respiration and vacuum experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and conducting experiments to test how changes in air rarity/density (and composition) affect animal respiration and survival using receivers, gauges, and related apparatus; includes measurement, observation, controls, and repeat trials across animal types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, volume-changeable, airtight receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a transparent receiver that is capable of changing its bulk without suffering any air to get in or out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes a receiver 'transparent, and be capable of changing its bulk without suffering any air to get in or out.' Practical solution given: a clear bladder (anointed with oil to increase transparency) tied to a fitted stopple and placed inside an outer glass receiver so the internal air can expand/contract while remaining sealed from external air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include and monitor a mercurial gauge to measure rarefaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a mercurial (mercury) gauge in the receiver to observe and mark the station of the mercury so you know the degree of rarefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the gauge so it is visible but protected from animal motion; observe the gauge to determine remaining fraction of air (e.g., 'it appeared by the gauge that there remained but half' or 'a fourth part'). Note that sometimes animals die without a sensible change in the gauge, so record gauge readings throughout the trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermetically seal apparatus to prevent air exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Seal the vessel hermetically so the imprisoned animal breathes no other air than that shut up at the time of inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods described include sealing the neck by heat (lamp) and bellows. Be aware that seals may be broken deliberately to reintroduce fresh air to attempt revival; also monitor for leaks via bladder intumescences and gauge readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify removed air by water displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how much air has been pumped out by allowing exterior air to force water into the receiver and measuring that water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after a dead viper was found, water was impelled into the cavity and then measured, showing four of five or five of six parts of the air had been pumped out. Use this as a quantitative check on the degree of evacuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bladder-inside-glass method to vary density while keeping composition constant
rubrics_metrics.description: To test effects of changing density while keeping the same portion of air, include the animal in a bladder inside an outer exhausted receiver so that pumping the outer receiver expands the bladder's air and rarefies it without introducing new air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedure: tie a fine thin bladder (air carefully expressed) to a phial's neck, place the phial in an external receiver with a gauge; pump the external receiver to expand the bladder and thus rarefy the internal air; reintroduce external air to compress bladder and restore density, observing revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design apparatus for visibility and to avoid opacity issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Make experimental vessels adequately transparent and arranged near a window so animal states are visible, and mitigate opacity (e.g., oiling bladder) that would obscure observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes opacity of bladders impeded observation and anoints them with oil; places apparatus near a window to see through both internal and external receivers. Opacity can hide signs of distress or recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record timing of symptoms, recoveries, and death precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure and record time intervals for onset of sickness, vomiting, breathing difficulty, fainting, recovery, and death (minutes to hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout: 'less than half a minute', 'end of the fourth minute', 'a full quarter of an hour', '60 hours', 'an hour or a little more', etc. Precise timing supports comparisons across trials and animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and log physiological and behavioral indicators of distress and recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for and record signs such as panting, shaking the head, vomiting, tremblings, convulsions, tongue motion, buoyancy changes, and motions indicative of life or death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple experiments cite these signs as indicators (e.g., greenfinch vomiting then recovering; mice trembling after recovery). Use these observations to infer stages of distress and whether revival occurs when density/composition changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for temperature vs composition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether changes in respiration outcomes are due to temperature or to the nature of the included air by applying refrigeration or heating as a control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An experiment immersed a sealed phial with a sick bird into very cold sal-ammoniac water for six minutes; refrigeration did not sensibly revive the bird, supporting the conclusion that something in the included air (not mere coldness) made it unfit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for contamination/clogging from animal effluviums
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider that the same air can become 'clogged and infected' by exhalations and excrementitious effluviums from the imprisoned animal, altering its fitness for respiration over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuefaction experiments deliberately reused the same air to test acclimation, but the author warns that buildup of effluvia may limit duration and require rest or fresh air; design trials to distinguish acclimation from degradation of the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat trials and test across multiple animal types
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiterate experiments and perform them on different sorts of animals to confirm generality (e.g., mice, birds, vipers, tadpoles, gnats, eels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes more trials and different animals are needed for 'further satisfaction' and reports both successes and unsuccessful attempts (e.g., tadpoles and gnats behaved differently). Document species-specific responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow rest periods between exposures for acclimation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing assuefaction (acclimation), provide rest/recovery intervals between exposures so the animal has time to recollect strength; gradual increases in rarefaction can extend tolerated durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: successive trials on one mouse with rest led from 4 minutes tolerance to keeping it a full quarter of an hour; subsequent trials with further rarefaction still produced recovery if rest was allowed. Track recovery quality (e.g., tremblings diminished after acclimation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controls and comparative setups to isolate causal factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise experiments that vary only one factor at a time (density vs fresh air introduction vs temperature) to attribute observed effects to that factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comparative experiments were run: using bladder to change density without adding fresh air; hermetically sealed vessels to keep composition constant; refrigeration to test temperature; comparing large vs small receivers; including gauge vs water-displacement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note and investigate bubble formation in tissues and fluids as a mechanistic factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and report the production and behavior of bubbles in blood, milk, gall, liver, and other soft parts upon withdrawal of air; consider their mechanical and physiological effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents blood 'boiling' into clusters, milk and gall intumescence, and bubbles issuing from cut fish parts and even a conspicuous bubble in a viper's eye. He hypothesizes bubbles may choke vessels, distort passages, irritate nerves, and hasten death — include such observations and consider them in causal explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent accidental ingress of air and note accidental events
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against accidental air getting in, since even a little ingress can alter outcomes; if accidental ingress occurs, pump out again or note its effect on vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a little air got in accidentally in one bird trial and animals recovered more than expected; monitor for and report accidental changes and their timing relative to observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When declaring death, attempt revival by reintroducing fresh air before final judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding an animal is dead, allow fresh air in (or break seal) and attempt to revive, as some animals show faint tokens of life after long apparent death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One mouse appeared quite dead after two and a half hours but showed faint tokens of life after the seal was broken and fresh air frequently blown in. Record any revival attempts and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and test alternative environmental hypotheses (e.g., toxic exhalations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a single mechanistic cause (e.g., thinness of air) — consider alternative causes such as poisonous or sulphureous steams and gather corroborative reports or tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author consults travellers' reports about mountain air and sulphureous exhalations causing sickness; uses refrigeration and other tests to discriminate hypotheses. Collect external observations and design targeted tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report unsuccessful attempts and methodological limitations candidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Document unsuccessful trials (e.g., failures to hatch animals in vacuum or to prevent the necessity of respiration) and limitations (opacity issues, difficulty of devices) for transparency and to guide further work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece explicitly labels some titles 'unsuccessful Attempt' and notes where particulars slipped memory; it recommends repeating trials and working with different animals. Include honest postscript remarks and future-work notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size apparatus relative to the organism and note scaling effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose receiver size appropriately relative to the animal; vessel size influences rate of distress and duration of survival and may interact with measurement sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in a comparatively large vessel a mouse 'seemed rather drooping than very near death' for two hours; in smaller vessels or with different volumes, timing differed. Report vessel volumes and relate to outcomes.
